title: The End of the Family Business (and What That Means for Your Deal)

 The End of the Family Business (and What That Means for Your Deal)
Hi Sara,
I’m a real deal attorney. I help people buy and sell businesses every day—especially in the accounting world, where things are getting a little... complicated.
Here’s a trend I’ve been seeing, and spoiler: it’s kind of a bummer.
Private equity has entered the room. And with it? Some serious downstream effects most people aren’t talking about—especially for family-run businesses.
Once upon a time, an accounting firm owner could slowly hand off the business to their child. A junior partner would earn their stripes, buy in over a decade, and one day—after a gold watch and a sentimental dinner—the torch would be passed.
That’s cute. It also doesn’t happen anymore.
Why not? Because valuations are up, interest rates are high, and most 25-year-olds working in their parent’s firm aren’t sitting on $3.5M in cash (shocking, I know). Meanwhile, sellers aren’t exactly eager to leave that kind of money on the table—especially when they can get 90% up front through SBA financing. 
So what happens? Do the parents forego millions of dollars prior to their retirement? Do they put that kind of debt on the shoulders of their children? 
I’ve now seen it five times in one year: parents skipping over their own kids and selling to third parties. The result? Adult children still working in the firm—except now they report to someone they’re not related to. Someone who bought their legacy.
It’s often a little bit sad. It’s messy. And if you’re buying one of these businesses, you need to tread carefully.
Here’s why it matters for you as a buyer:
Family dynamics are tricky. You’re stepping into the middle of a deeply personal transition. Be ready to manage with a lot of emotional intelligence.

Client loyalty often sticks to the family. If Josh Williams III has been the familiar face for 15 years, clients may not take kindly to your new ownership—even if you paid top dollar.

Legal vulnerability. You can get the seller to sign a non-compete, but their adult child? Depending on the state, you might not be able to get them under one at all. And if they’re not? They’re free to walk out and compete.

So no, you’re not just buying a practice. You’re buying a set of relationships, and some of them may walk out the door on Day 1.
Bottom line: If you’re buying a family business, dig deeper than the P&L. Understand the people. Secure the key team.

To strong offers and smoother transitions,
Sara Sharp
